module_title: Setting Up a Spawn Production Laboratory

lessons.title: Designing a Clean Room and Laminar Flow Hood
lessons.body: A clean room is the heart of spawn production. You need a space where airborne contaminants are minimised. In Africa, you can convert a small room (2m x 3m) by sealing windows, doors, and cracks. Use plastic sheeting or epoxy paint on walls and floors for easy cleaning. Install a simple ventilation system with a HEPA filter (at least H13 grade) to create positive pressure. A laminar flow hood is your workbench for inoculations. You can build a DIY hood using a box fan, a HEPA filter, and a plastic storage box. Place the fan to blow filtered air across your work area. Ensure the hood is in a draft-free corner. For a professional setup, buy a horizontal laminar flow hood (about $500-$1500). Always clean the hood with 70% alcohol before use. The clean room should have a foot-operated door or a double-door entry to reduce contamination. Keep the room free of clutter. Wear clean lab coats and gloves. In humid African climates, use a dehumidifier to keep humidity below 60%. Test your clean room by exposing agar plates for 15 minutes; if more than 2 colonies appear, improve your filtration. This setup costs between $200 (DIY) and $3000 (professional).

lessons.title: Essential Laboratory Equipment and Tools
lessons.body: To produce spawn, you need specific tools. First, a pressure cooker or autoclave for sterilisation (see next lesson). Second, a still air box (SAB) or laminar flow hood for inoculations. Third, a gas burner or alcohol lamp for flaming tools. Fourth, inoculation loops or scalpels for transferring mycelium. Fifth, petri dishes or culture slants for growing mother cultures. Sixth, spawn bags or bottles (polypropylene bags with filter patches) for grain spawn. Seventh, a grain cooker or pot for preparing grains. Eighth, a thermometer and hygrometer to monitor conditions. Ninth, a scale (0.1g accuracy) for measuring ingredients. Tenth, a pH meter or test strips. You also need 70% isopropyl alcohol, bleach, and gloves. In Africa, you can source many items locally: pressure cookers from markets, polypropylene bags from agricultural suppliers, and grains (wheat, sorghum, millet) from farmers. A basic setup costs $300-$800. Buy a used autoclave if new is too expensive. Ensure all equipment is clean and stored in a dry place. Keep a logbook for maintenance.

lessons.title: Sterilization Equipment: Autoclave and Pressure Cooker
lessons.body: Sterilisation kills all contaminants. You need either an autoclave or a pressure cooker. Autoclaves use steam under pressure (15 psi, 121Â°C) for 15-30 minutes. Pressure cookers work similarly but are cheaper. In Africa, a 20-litre pressure cooker costs $50-$150. For spawn production, you need a cooker that reaches 15 psi. Use a weight gauge or pressure dial. Sterilise grain spawn for 90 minutes at 15 psi. For agar media, sterilise for 20 minutes. Always add water to the cooker (about 2-3 litres) and place jars on a rack. Let pressure drop naturally before opening. Do not open hot. For larger scale, buy a vertical autoclave (50-100 litres) for $1000-$3000. You can also use a drum steriliser with a fire underneath, but it's less reliable. Test sterility by incubating a sample of sterilised grain in a jar for 3 days; if no growth, it's good. Always use heat-resistant gloves. In areas with unreliable electricity, use gas or firewood. Maintain your equipment: clean seals, check gauges, and replace parts as needed. This is the most critical step for contamination-free spawn.

lessons.title: Incubation Room Setup and Environmental Control
lessons.body: After inoculation, spawn bags need a dark, warm, and clean incubation room. Ideal temperature for most mushrooms (oyster, shiitake) is 24-28Â°C. In Africa, you can use a small room with insulation. If too hot, use a fan or air conditioner; if too cold, use a heater. Humidity should be 60-70%. Use a hygrometer and humidifier if needed. Keep the room dark; light can trigger premature fruiting. Shelving should be metal or plastic, not wood (which harbours mould). Allow 30 cm between bags for air circulation. Monitor daily for contamination (green, black, or pink spots). Remove contaminated bags immediately. Incubate for 10-21 days depending on species. For a small setup, a cabinet with a thermostat works. For larger, a room with a split AC and humidifier costs $500-$2000. In rural areas, use a cool cupboard or a hole in the ground? No, better to build a simple insulated box. Always keep the room clean: wipe shelves with bleach weekly. Keep a log of temperature and humidity. This control ensures fast, healthy mycelium growth.

lessons.title: Safety Protocols and Contamination Prevention
lessons.body: Safety is paramount. Always wear gloves, lab coat, and mask when working with chemicals or in the clean room. Use 70% alcohol for surface sterilisation; it's flammable, so keep away from flames. Bleach (10% solution) is for floors and walls. Never mix bleach with ammonia. For contamination prevention: work in a still air box or laminar flow hood. Flame your tools until red hot. Cool them on agar or in a sterile area. Minimise movement and talking. Keep petri dishes closed. Use sterile technique: open lids only slightly, work quickly. Sterilise all media and tools. Clean the room before and after work. Have a foot bath with bleach at the entrance. Quarantine any contaminated cultures. Dispose of contaminated bags by autoclaving or burning. Train all workers in aseptic technique. Keep a first aid kit for cuts and burns. In Africa, be aware of power cuts; have a backup plan for sterilisation. Regular training and strict protocols reduce contamination rates to under 5%. Without these, you can lose entire batches.

lessons.title: Budgeting for Lab Setup and Operations
lessons.body: Starting a spawn lab requires careful budgeting. For a small-scale lab (producing 100 bags per week), initial costs: clean room conversion ($200-$500), laminar flow hood ($500-$1500), pressure cooker ($100-$200), incubation room ($300-$800), and tools ($200-$400). Total initial: $1300-$3400. Operational costs per month: grains ($50-$100), bags ($20-$50), electricity/gas ($30-$100), and labour ($100-$300). Consumables like alcohol, bleach, gloves: $50. Total monthly: $250-$600. You can reduce costs by DIY hood ($50), using a pressure cooker instead of autoclave, and sourcing grains locally. Revenue: spawn sells for $2-$5 per bag. Selling 400 bags per month gives $800-$2000. Profit margin is high after initial investment. In Africa, consider microfinance loans or grants. Keep records of all expenses. Start small and scale. A break-even point is typically 3-6 months. Always set aside 10% for repairs and replacements. This budget ensures you don't run out of funds mid-production.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a clean room in spawn production?
quiz.explanation: A clean room reduces airborne contaminants that can spoil spawn.

quiz.q: Which grade of HEPA filter is recommended for a clean room?
quiz.explanation: H13 HEPA filters capture 99.95% of particles, ensuring clean air.

quiz.q: What is a laminar flow hood used for?
quiz.explanation: A laminar flow hood provides a sterile work area for inoculation.

quiz.q: How can you test if your clean room is working properly?
options: A) Expose agar plates for 15 minutes
quiz.explanation: Agar plates exposed to air will show contamination if the room is not clean.

quiz.q: What is a still air box (SAB) used for?
quiz.explanation: A still air box provides a sterile environment for inoculation when a hood is unavailable.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT essential lab equipment for spawn production?
quiz.explanation: A refrigerator is not essential; spawn incubation requires warmth, not cold.

quiz.q: What type of bags are commonly used for grain spawn?
options: B) Polypropylene bags with filter patches
quiz.explanation: Polypropylene bags withstand sterilisation and have filters for gas exchange.

quiz.q: Why is a scale with 0.1g accuracy important?
quiz.explanation: Precise measurement of ingredients ensures consistent media and spawn quality.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sterilisation time for grain spawn at 15 psi?
quiz.explanation: 90 minutes at 15 psi ensures complete sterilisation of grain spawn.

quiz.q: What pressure should a pressure cooker reach for effective sterilisation?
quiz.explanation: 15 psi (121Â°C) is the standard for sterilising mushroom media.

quiz.q: How can you test if your sterilisation was successful?
options: B) Incubate a sample for 3 days
quiz.explanation: Incubating a sample shows if any contaminants survived sterilisation.

quiz.q: What should you do before opening a pressure cooker after sterilisation?
quiz.explanation: Letting pressure drop naturally prevents sudden boiling and injury.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for incubating most mushroom spawn?
quiz.explanation: Most mushroom mycelium grows best at 24-28Â°C.

quiz.q: Why should incubation rooms be kept dark?
quiz.explanation: Light can trigger fruiting before the spawn is fully colonised.

quiz.q: What humidity level is recommended for an incubation room?
quiz.explanation: 60-70% humidity prevents bags from drying out without promoting mould.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see green mould in a spawn bag?
quiz.explanation: Contaminated bags must be removed to prevent spread.

quiz.q: What material is best for shelving in an incubation room?
quiz.explanation: Metal or plastic shelves are easy to clean and do not harbour mould.

quiz.q: How often should you clean incubation room shelves?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning with bleach prevents contamination buildup.

quiz.q: What is the correct concentration of alcohol for surface sterilisation?
quiz.explanation: 70% alcohol is most effective at killing microbes.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing bleach with ammonia?
quiz.explanation: Mixing bleach and ammonia creates dangerous chlorine gas.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a foot bath at the lab entrance?
quiz.explanation: A bleach foot bath reduces contaminants brought in on shoes.

quiz.q: How should you sterilise metal tools during inoculation?
quiz.explanation: Flaming tools until red hot ensures sterility.

quiz.q: What should you do with contaminated bags?
quiz.explanation: Autoclaving or burning kills contaminants and prevents spread.

quiz.q: What is a key safety practice when working in the lab?
options: A) Wear gloves and lab coat
quiz.explanation: Gloves and lab coat protect you and prevent contamination.

quiz.q: What is the approximate initial cost for a small-scale spawn lab?
quiz.explanation: A small lab setup costs between $1300 and $3400.

quiz.q: Which item can be sourced locally to reduce costs?
quiz.explanation: Pressure cookers are widely available in local markets.

quiz.q: What is the typical selling price for one spawn bag?
quiz.explanation: Spawn bags typically sell for $2-$5 each.

quiz.q: What is the break-even period for a spawn lab?
quiz.explanation: Most labs break even within 3-6 months of operation.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of expenses?
quiz.explanation: Records help you monitor costs and ensure profitability.

quiz.q: What percentage of budget should be set aside for repairs?
quiz.explanation: Setting aside 10% for repairs prevents financial strain.
